hook: If your memory feels unreliable — forgetting words mid-sentence, losing your train of thought — that's not aging. That's what chronic light sleep does to the hippocampus.
topic: Sleep and memory consolidation — N2, slow-wave, and hippocampal transfer
body:
**Forgetting words mid-sentence. Re-reading the same paragraph four times. Losing your train of thought in a conversation you were just following. If this is your normal — it is almost certainly a sleep problem, not an age problem.**

Here's what's happening inside the brain. During N2 sleep — the stage that makes up roughly half of your total sleep time — the brain produces structures called sleep spindles. These are brief bursts of neural activity, and their job is to coordinate the transfer of information from the hippocampus, your short-term memory store, to the cortex for long-term storage.

When your sleep is repeatedly fragmented or cut short, that transfer doesn't complete. You encoded the information during the day. It was sitting in your hippocampus. But it never made it into long-term storage. So it feels like the memory was never formed — because, architecturally, it wasn't.

You don't have a memory problem. You have an N2 deficit. Those are not the same thing, and only one of them has a fix.

The field guide covering this in full is linked in my bio.
